title: Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids and mortality risk in depression: immune-inflammatory mediation in NHANES 1999–2018

sections.abstract:
Immune-inflammatory deregulation in depression may contribute to elevated risk of subsequent mortality. While dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), docosapentaenoic acid (DPA), and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), are known to confer neuroprotective effects for their anti-inflammatory properties, population-based evidence regarding their survival benefits and underlying mechanisms in depression remain scarce. This study aimed to investigate association between dietary omega-3 PUFAs and mortality risk in depressed individuals and identify immune-inflammatory mediation underlying mortality reductions.

Totally, 6,782 depressed individuals aged 20 years and above in 10 cycles (1999–2018) of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) were analyzed. Omega-3 PUFAs intake (total and individual) was assessed through 24-hour dietary recalls. Cox proportional hazard models were used to calculated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for morality risk across omega-3 PUFA quartiles. Quantile-based g-computation model determined individual PUFA contributions, while mediation analysis evaluated the role of Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI) and Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index (SII) in mortality reductions.

Over the follow-up period of 679,294 person years, 1,281 deaths were documented. The HRs for the highest versus lowest quartile of omega-3 PUFAs were 0.76 (95% CI: 0.62, 0.94) for total mortality, 0.72 (95% CI: 0.50, 1.02) for CVD mortality, 0.82 (95% CI: 0.50, 1.35) for cancer mortality, and 0.77 (95% CI: 0.59, 1.00) for other-cause mortality. DPA showed the strongest association (58.40% weight for total mortality reduction, P = 0.002; 59.80% for other causes, P = 0.011), while EPA contributed most to cardiovascular mortality reductions (60.4%, P = 0.046). Mediation analysis revealed GNRI accounted for 8.1% of PUFA-mortality association (10.5% for DPA), with SII mediating 6.9% of DPA-specific benefit.

Higher intake of omega-3 PUFAs, predominantly EPA and DPA, were associated with a lower mortality risk in depressed individuals, partially mediated by immune-nutritional pathways. These findings underscore omega-3 PUFAs as potential dietary adjuncts for improving survival in depression through immunomodulation. Further long-term clinical studies are warranted to validate the survival benefits of omega-3 PUFAs in patients with depression.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12937-025-01265-8.

Keywords: Depression, Omega-3 PUFAs, Mortality, Inflammation, GNRI, NHANES
sections.introduction:
Depression represents a global health priority, affecting over 280 million individuals and ranking as a leading cause of disability worldwide, particularly in low- and middle-income countries [ 1 ]. Beyond its well-documented psychological burden, depression exhibits robust bidirectional associations with cardiovascular disease (CVD) and neoplastic disorders [ 2 , 3 ]. The pathophysiological interconnections significantly worsen prognostic outcomes, as further manifested by increased mortality rates [ 4 , 5 ], diminished life expectancy [ 6 ], and heightened suicide risk [ 7 , 8 ]. Mitigating this multifaceted public health challenge demands integrated strategies encompassing medical care, psychosocial support, and behavioral interventions.

Mounting evidence implicates immune-mediated inflammation as a key driver of depression pathogenesis [ 9 ]. Patients with depressive disorders consistently exhibit elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), compared to healthy individuals [ 10 ]. The cytokines may disrupt blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity [ 11 ], impair neurotransmitter signal and neuroplasticity [ 12 ], and dysregulate hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity [ 13 ]. This immune-inflammatory cascade manifests as clinical sickness behavior, characterized by fatigue, anhedonia, and cognitive dysfunction. Peripheral immune alterations further support this link, including shifts in white blood cell (WBC) subsets (e.g., monocytes and neutrophils) [ 14 ]. Composite biomarkers like the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) and geriatric nutritional risk index (GNRI), integrated WBC subsets with platelet counts and albumin levels as novel indicators of immune-inflammatory dysregulation in depression [ 15 , 16 ].

Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), primarily eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), docosapentaenoic acid (DPA), and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), exert neuroprotective effects through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory mechanisms [ 17 – 19 ], including neurotransmitter signal modulation [ 20 ] and neuroplasticity enhancement [ 21 ]. Emerging evidence further reveals that EPA has superior efficacy in mitigating depressive symptoms via cytokine regulation [ 22 , 23 ], DPA reduces cardiovascular risk through immune pathway modulations [ 24 ], while DHA is crucial for maintaining brain cell membrane integrity and cognitive function [ 25 ]. However, critical gaps persist in understanding clinical translational implications of omega-3 PUFAs in depression. This population faces elevated mortality risks linked to chronic inflammation and metabolic dysregulation, yet the longitudinal effects of omega-3 PUFAs intake on survival outcomes, and the mediating role of immune-inflammatory pathways, remain unquantified.

This study aimed to (1) examine the prospective association between dietary intake of total and individual omega-3 PUFAs and mortality risk in depressed individuals, and (2) investigate the mediating role of nutrition-driven immune-inflammatory pathways in this longitudinal association. Utilizing data from the NHANES cohort, this prospective study would provide novel mechanistic insights into how dietary omega-3 PUFAs may modulate immune-inflammatory responses to improve survival in depressed individuals.
sections.discussion:
To our knowledge, this is the first population-based study to examine the differential associations and their potential mediation pathways of dietary omega-3 PUFAs, specifically EPA, DPA, and DHA, with mortality risk in the depressed individuals, using a large, nationally representative cohort with comprehensive adjustment for potential confounders. Our findings revealed a significant and inverse association between dietary omega-3 PUFAs and mortality, with EPA specifically linked to reduced cardiovascular mortality and DPA associated with decreased other-cause mortality. These apparent survival benefits of omega-3 PUFAs were partially mediated by their ability to reduce nutritional risk (GNRI) among older participants, while evidence for inflammatory mediation was specifically limited to the DPA-SII pathway. The absence of significant mediation by the PNI indicated that immunomodulation may not be a primary mediation for the PUFA-mortality associations.

Our primary findings supported that higher intake of omega-3 PUFAs was associated with a lower risk of mortality in depressed participants. More favorable attention has been consistently received in the general populations and those at high CVD risk, but limited data are directed towards the depressed individuals [ 17 , 41 ]. In the SADHART-CHF trial, higher plasma levels of omega-3 PUFAs led to a long-term survival rate in the patients with depression comorbid heart failure [ 42 ]. The improved cardiac function and depressive symptoms were similarly seen in another trial of omega-3 PUFAs supplementations [ 43 ]. Compared with evidence of the prior studies, our data indicated that EPA, DHA, and DPA did not equally influence mortality risk in the depressed individuals, as shown by EPA and DPA rather than DHA being the main factors associated with reduced mortality in depressed individuals. This finding may have been substantially underlined by the antidepressive evidence from many pre-clinical and clinical trials. Recent emerging evidence suggests that EPA-derived endocannabinoids exert more antidepressant effects than those derived from DHA through a potent anti-inflammatory and vasodilatory properties [ 44 , 45 ]. Of note, DPA, endogenously synthesized from EPA, may affect mortality via its cardioprotective potential [ 46 ] We observed that mortality-lowering association of DPA is similar to those of EPA rather than DHA, which may be explained by the well-established fact that DPA can be retro-converted to EPA, whereas it cannot readily metabolize into DHA due to rate-limiting enzymes in vivo [ 47 ] The need for further clinical trials are underscored to explore the differential effects of individual omega-3 PUFAs on long-term survival rates and the underlying mechanisms involved.

Subgroup analyses indicated that omega-3 PUFAs were associated with greater reductions in mortality risk among middle-aged and elderly individuals compared to younger ones. The levels of omega-3 PUFAs in erythrocytes and plasma/serum are found to be relatively higher in the oldest compared to the youngest [ 48 ]. This may have caused more favorable alteration in those atherosclerosis progression, brain volume atrophy and ultimately neurocognitive decline [ 48 , 49 ], perhaps ascribing to a reduction of PUFAs in cell membranes, higher intestinal absorption during aging, high availability and release of adipose tissue stocks [ 48 ]. We also found the omega-3 PUFAs were associated with lower cardiovascular mortality in non-smokers, implying that smoking might undermine cardioprotective effects of these fatty acids. Intriguingly, among smokers, omega-3 PUFAs were evidently linked to reduced cancer mortality. This could potentially be attributed to omega-3 PUFAs’ anti-inflammatory properties that may at least benefit cancer prognosis [ 50 ].

We focused on a series of the nutritional and immune-inflammatory markers as potential mediators due to the well-established role of omega-3 PUFAs in reducing inflammation [ 51 ] and enhancing nutritional immunomodulation [ 52 ]. In our study, SII and GNRI modestly mediated the mortality risk reduction of EPA and DPA in depressed individuals. Of note, more than 60% of the depressed participants were the middle-aged and elderly, who may have often suffered from malnutrition due to accelerated catabolism during aging that reduced albumin and muscle mass. GNRI, as calculated using the serum albumin level and BMI, is a more reliable nutrition-related risk index in predicting the morbidity and mortality in relation to pathologies in elderly patients than are indexes that use albumin or BMI alone. Heart failure patients at both high-EPA and high-GNRI levels had a remarkably higher event-free survival rate than those at either high-GNRI or high-EPA levels [ 53 ]. Furthermore, SII combines peripheral lymphocyte, neutrophil and platelet counts to indicate an integrated mechanisms involving the immune-inflammatory process, which are well validated in predicting clinical prognosis in diseased patients including depression [ 15 , 54 ] and CVD [ 55 , 56 ]. A RCT enrolled patients with gastric cancer who underwent elective radical gastrectomy showed supplemental omega-3 PUFAs recover patients’ inflammatory-immune function by reducing lymphocyte counts and increasing albumin and pre-albumin levels [ 57 ]. In supporting of this comment, our data also found the inverse association between PUFAs and mortality risk may be partly explained by their ability to modulate the immune inflammation. Collective data from the prior studies and our medicating analyses may help to suggest the interplay between nutritional and immune-inflammatory mediation underscores the complex comorbid mechanisms how omega-3 PUFAs exerted beneficial impacts on mortality in the depressed individuals.

We also found that the CHF-related events slightly mediated the protective associations of EPA with cardiovascular mortality. In CHF patients, the coexistence of inflammation and myocardial fibrosis is causally linked to cardiac dysfunction, which enables them to have a poor prognosis such as ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac fibrosis, thereby potentially raising the risk of sudden death [ 58 ]. Recent meta-analyses have suggested that omega-3 PUFAs especially EPA improve cardiac fibrosis in CHF through reducing cholesterol crystal formation [ 59 ], oxidative modification of atherogenic lipoproteins [ 60 ]. Moreover, EPA may lower cardiac fibrosis through inhibiting the synthesis of 2-series pro-inflammatory prostaglandin derived from omega-6 arachidonic acid [ 61 ]. The potentials to reduce inflammation-induced fibroblast cell communications in CHF were found to be mediated by the PUFAs’ multi-targets such as NRF2, FFAR4, and GPR120 [ 62 ], which were likely to ultimately contribute to a protection against cardiac death. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that our observation of the CHF-related event as a mediator might be a false positive. Since death from the CHF event is part of all-cause death, the results on CHF as a mediator need cautious interpretation.

Our study has some potential limitations. The observational design of this study inherently limits our ability to establish causality. As such, the current findings should be interpreted with prudence. Additionally, dietary omega-3 PUFAs in depressed participants were assessed through 24-hour recall, which may have introduced recall bias and report errors, compared to blood-based biomarkers that could more accurately reflect the real intake levels. Second, individuals’ dietary habits might have changed during the follow-up period. This could potentially disrupt the direction of the association estimates. Notwithstanding these challenges, our data indicated an increasing trend in dietary intake of omega-3 PUFAs in US depressed participants from 1999 to 2018, which may help explain the associations observed in the present study. Third, due to the presence of missing lipid data and limited number of cardiovascular indicators measured, our study was unable to fully clarify the PUFAs’ cardioprotective mediation in depression. Future laboratory research may explore the potential mechanisms of omega-3 PUFAs in preventing against the comorbidity of CVD and depression. Furthermore, although subgroup analyses showed consistent associations across NHANES cycles utilizing different depression assessment instruments, inherent psychometric variations between these diagnostic tools may introduce some degree of classification bias. Fourth, while our study was conducted among U.S. adults, the generalizability of our findings might be restricted to other populations. The mediation effects of the inflammatory and nutritional modulation need also to be investigated in another population-based cohort. Finally, despite multiple adjustments for numerous unbalance variable at baseline, residual confounders and unmeasurable factors might persist. As a result, the findings based on the NHANES cohort necessitate a repetition in another cohort or validation in large-scale RCTs.
sections.conclusion: Higher dietary intake of EPA and DPA was significantly associated with reduced mortality risk in depressed individuals, partially mediated by their nutritional-inflammatory modulating properties. Such findings underscore the potential of omega-3 PUFAs as dietary adjuncts in subsequent mortality reductions among depressed individuals. Future randomized clinical trials are warranted to elucidate the survival benefits and potential mechanism of omega-3 PUFAs in depression.
